# The biology of C. richardii as a tool to understand plant evolution

## Authors

- Sylvia P Kinosian<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-0918-7196](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0918-7196)) †
- Paul G Wolf<sup>2</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-4317-6976](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4317-6976))

### Affiliations

1. Negaunee Institute for Plant Conservation Science, Chicago Botanic Garden Chicago United States
2. Department of Biological Sciences, University of Alabama Huntsville United States ([ROR:03xrrjk67](https://ror.org/03xrrjk67))

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

The fern Ceratopteris richardii has been studied as a model organism for over 50 years because it is easy to grow and has a short life cycle. In particular, as the first homosporous vascular plant for which genomic resources were developed, C. richardii has been an important system for studying plant evolution. However, we know relatively little about the natural history of C. richardii. In this article, we summarize what is known about this aspect of C. richardii, and discuss how learning more about its natural history could greatly increase our understanding of the evolution of land plants.

## Introduction

The genus Ceratopteris has a long and complicated taxonomic history. It was first described by Linnaeus under the genus Acrostichum (Linnaeus, 1764), and the name Ceratopteris was later assigned by Brongniart (Brongniart, 1821). Since then, Ceratopteris has been placed in a number of different families, with the number of species within the genus ranging between one and twelve (Lloyd, 1974). Today it is placed within Pteridaceae, one of the largest and most diverse fern families (PPG, 2016; Figure 1).

There are about ten species within Ceratopteris, which can be found throughout the tropics (Figure 2; Masuyama and Watano, 2010; Zhang et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2021). The classification of these species was made difficult by their inconsistent morphologies, and molecular methods were needed to reconstruct a backbone phylogeny for the genus (Adjie et al., 2007; Kinosian et al., 2020a). Recent work has shown that cryptic and hybrid species may be quite common in Ceratopteris, warranting a more rigorous evaluation of the relationships between species in the genus (e.g., Kinosian et al., 2020b).

Ceratopteris richardii was first developed as a model system for ferns in the 1960s and 70s, primarily because it was easy to grow in the lab and had a short life cycle (Figure 2; Pal and Pal, 1962; Pal and Pal, 1963; Klekowski, 1970; Stein, 1971; Hickok, 1973; Hickok and Klekowski, 1973; Lloyd and Warne, 1978). Many studies used spores from a Cuban vouchered collection, now known as the Hnn strain or C-fern (Hickok, 1977). Additional strains of C. richardii and the species C. thalictroides and C. pteridoides have since been developed (Hickok and Klekowski, 1974; Nakazato et al., 2006; Muthukumar et al., 2013). In the past few decades, Ceratopteris has become an important model in the study of sex determination (Eberle et al., 1995; Ganger et al., 2019; Atallah et al., 2018; Banks, 1997), apogamy (Bui et al., 2017; Cordle et al., 2010), genome structure (Nakazato et al., 2006; Baniaga and Barker, 2019), hybridization (Hickok and Klekowski, 1974; Adjie et al., 2007), reproductive barriers (Nakazato et al., 2007), developmental biology (Hou and Hill, 2002; Conway and Di Stilio, 2020; Sun and Li, 2020; Aragón-Raygoza et al., 2020), and transgenic studies in ferns (Plackett et al., 2018; Bui et al., 2015; Cannon et al., 2018).

Ceratopteris richardii is one of few spore-bearing model systems (e.g., Physcomitrella: Cove, 2005; Rensing et al., 2008; Selaginella: Banks et al., 2011) and the only vascular spore-bearing homosporous model species, making it a critical evolutionary lineage in comparative studies (see Box 1 for a glossary of terms used in this article). Compared to other model plants, Ceratopteris has a large genome (~11 GB) and high base chromosome number (n = 39), which has partly caused genetic resources for C. richardii to lag behind those of other plant model systems, delaying such comparative work.

Recently, however, the first draft genome sequence for C. richardii was published (Marchant, 2019a), which was the first for a homosporous fern. Ceratopteris richardii was chosen for sequencing because, although it has a large genome compared to other plants, it is relatively small for a homosporous fern (Sessa et al., 2014; Marchant et al., 2019b).

Having a reference genome for C. richardii expands its research potential and builds on decades of previous work. A homosporous plant genome provides the opportunity for exploring and comparing various aspects of plant biology such as the alternation of generations, sex determination, and reproductive modes between heterosporous and homosporous plants. In addition, a reference genome for Ceratopteris is beneficial for the development of new markers in targeted gene sequencing or whole-genome resequencing. In turn, this makes incorporating wild collections into genomic research much easier and will help us gain a more nuanced understanding of the biology, ecology, and evolutionary history of Ceratopteris.

## The variable natural history of Ceratopteris

The model species Ceratopteris richardii originates in the Caribbean and Western Africa, and grows rooted or floating in shallow water (Figure 2). Indeed, all species within Ceratopteris grow in or near areas in the tropics that become inundated seasonally (Figures 2 and 3), mostly growing in fresh water, though they can tolerate salt water (Lloyd, 1974; Warne and Hickok, 1987).

Its sister genus, Acrostichum, is well-known for being able to tolerate high levels of salt as it grows in tidal and intertidal habitats (Zhang et al., 2013; Medina et al., 1990). The extent of natural salt tolerance in Ceratopteris is not fully understood, but salt-tolerant mutants of C. richardii are easy to generate in the lab (Chasan, 1992; Warne et al., 1995). Continuing to study salt tolerance in Ceratopteris may be beneficial in understanding the genetic mechanisms of this trait, or applying such findings to crop systems in the future.

Through much of its range, Ceratopteris inhabits ephemeral water sources. To reproduce in this fleeting habitat C. richardii has a short life cycle of about 120 days (Stein, 1971), which is much shorter than almost all ferns’ annual or multi-year life cycles. The fern life cycle, like that of all land plants, is characterized by the alternation of generations between the diploid sporophyte and haploid gametophyte. Following fertilization, a diploid zygote is formed that is temporarily reliant on the gametophyte and becomes self-sufficient over time. In the fern life cycle, the gametophyte and sporophyte generations are completely separate at certain stages. Comparatively, in bryophytes, the sporophyte generation is entirely dependent on the gametophyte, and the opposite is true in seed plants. The fern life cycle provides an opportunity to study sporophyte and gametophyte generation separately, something that is not possible in other lineages of plants.

Because ferns have independent and free-living sporophytic and gametophytic phases, there are multiple ways in which the life cycle of Ceratopteris can proceed (Haufler et al., 2016). Fertilization can occur via gametes from different plants (sporophytic outcrossing), gametes from the same plant but different gametophytes (gametophytic outcrossing), and also gametes from the same gametophyte (gametophytic selfing). Studies show evidence of outcrossing within (Nakazato et al., 2007) and among species of Ceratopteris (i.e., hybridization, Adjie et al., 2007; Kinosian et al., 2020a; Hickok and Klekowski, 1974).

Outcrossing and gametophytic sex expression in ferns is often controlled by pheromones known as antheridiogens. These gibberellin-related chemicals are released by early-germinating archegoniate gametophytes to promote antheridiate gametophyte development in immature gametophytes. This pheromone system confers some of the benefits of heterospory to homosporous plants, namely outcrossing (Bateman and DiMichele, 1994; Hornych et al., 2021). In the case of Ceratopteris, however, solitary gametophytes can also become bisexual and self-fertilize; therefore, theoretically, only one spore can colonize new habitats (Schedlbauer and Klekowski, 1972). This is the case for many ferns and aids Ceratopteris as a model organism because studies can be designed around this flexible life history.

In addition, asexual reproduction (apomixis) can be induced in C. richardii in the lab (Cordle et al., 2007). The variation within the life cycle of Ceratopteris makes it a powerful system in which to study reproduction in ferns, as well as an evolutionary point of reference for understanding reproduction in seed plants.

Ceratopteris was developed as a model organism for many of the same reasons as other model systems. It is easy to grow in a lab setting, has a rapid life cycle that makes experiments tangible, and is tractable for genetic transformations (Eberle et al., 1995; Hickok et al., 1995). Model organisms are often chosen for convenience, but that can make them poor representative taxa (Alfred and Baldwin, 2015).

In the case of Ceratopteris, it has several traits that are very unusual among ferns. For example, it is one of only a handful of semi-aquatic species out of around 12,000 extant ferns (PPG, 2016). The life cycle of Ceratopteris, while beneficial for lab experiments, is incredibly short for a fern (Stein, 1971). Finally, it has half or a quarter of the number of spores typical for a leptosporangiate fern: most leptosporangiate ferns produce 64 spores per sporangium, whereas species in Ceratopteris produce 32 or 16 spores per sporangium (Lloyd, 1974). This is important because a spore number of 32 or 16 is often indicative of apogamy (Grusz, 2016), but no natural apogamous taxa have been described in Ceratopteris. These characteristics, among others, make Ceratopteris a good model species but not necessarily an accurate representation of all ferns.

## A transgenic model for seed-free plants

Free-living generations and a flexible life cycle make Ceratopteris an important model for evolutionary developmental studies. A reference ontogenetic framework for the Hnn strain of C. richardii (C-fern; Hickok et al., 1995) was recently published, detailing the development of the gametophyte and sporophyte, providing an important reference for future work (Conway and Di Stilio, 2020). This reference, in combination with stable transformation techniques, plus a C. richardii transcriptome (Geng et al., 2021; Atallah et al., 2018) and genome (Marchant et al., 2022; Marchant et al., 2019b) now provide the necessary suite of tools for comparative work.

In the Hnn strain of Ceratopteris richardii stable transgenic lines have been established in both the gametophyte and sporophyte generations. Transformation of the tissue in these plants has been accomplished by bombardment of sporophytic tissue by tungsten microparticles (Plackett et al., 2014; Plackett et al., 2015a), Agrobacterium infection of haploid gametophyte tissue (Bui et al., 2015), and agrobacterium infection of haploid spores (Muthukumar et al., 2013).

Transformation on gametophytes provides an important perspective on gene function in the haploid generation, something that is not as easy in seed plants. Another benefit of working with transformed gametophytes is that they can self-fertilize to produce sporophytes that are stable homozygotes. However, this can also be accomplished if transformation is done on sporophytes. Spores can be collected and screening of resulting gametophytes can then be used to produce stable homozygous transgenic lines via gametophytic selfing.

Thus, transgenic lines of C. richardii have been developed, and allow for comparative studies of gene function and evolution across land plants in both the gametophyte and sporophyte generations. The ability to have transgenic lines in both generations provides a unique perspective for studying how genes, growth conditions, or other factors affect sporophytes and gametophytes differently.

A recent study using both transgenic gametophytes and sporophytes of Ceratopteris investigated the role of the LEAFY transcription factor (LFY) in development (Plackett et al., 2018). LFY is important for cell division in moss embryos (Tanahashi et al., 2005) and angiosperm floral meristem development (Carpenter and Coen, 1990). While it is known to be important in both of these lineages, there is no functional overlap between mosses and angiosperms, so understanding the evolutionary history of LFY has been challenging.

Ceratopteris provides an evolutionary and functional midpoint with which to study the role of the LFY gene in development. Using several transgenic lines of C. richardii, Plackett et al. evaluated the role of LFY in sporophyte development. They also reported, for the first time in any land plant, that LFY function is required for C. richardii gametophyte development (Plackett et al., 2018). This suggests that LFY was important for gametophyte development for the last common ancestor of ferns and seed plants, but this function was lost in seed plants where the gametophyte is greatly reduced (Plackett et al., 2018). Incorporating other vegetative developmental systems into further studies with C. richardii (e.g., Vasco et al., 2013; Vasco et al., 2016; Hernández-Hernández et al., 2021) will help us gain a more nuanced understanding of these processes across land plants.

Similarly, there is a growing body of work on the developmental patterns associated with reproduction using Ceratopteris. It is well-established that apogamy can be induced in C. richardii (Cordle et al., 2007), but the genetic mechanism responsible was unknown until recently. In flowering plants, BABY-BOOM (BBM) genes promote somatic embryogenesis (Boutilier et al., 2002; Soriano et al., 2013). These genes are absent in non-seed plants, but an ortholog of the BBM gene AINTEGUMENTA was identified in C. richardii (Bui et al., 2017). Using Agrobacterium-mediated transformations, Bui et al., created C. richardii gametophytes with both over- and knockdown-expression of the apogamy-inducing gene, CrANT. This was the first such study conducted in a non-seed plant and provides evidence for conserved gene function in apomixis across land plant lineages (Bui et al., 2017).

Future work using transgenic lines of Ceratopteris richardii has the potential to connect gene expression and function across land plants. Work has already been done on many gene families in model bryophytes, the lycophyte Selaginella, and seed plants. As mentioned above, however, there is not always functional overlap between these lineages. Including Ceratopteris may provide such a functional or developmental link. It is important to note that ferns like Ceratopteris are an independent lineage with unique development characteristics that have continued to evolve since diverging from other land plants, as are bryophytes and seed plants (Plackett et al., 2015b; McDaniel, 2021). However, Ceratopteris does share many characteristics with bryophytes (e.g., spores, independent gametophyte generation) and seed plants (e.g., vasculature, independent sporophyte generation), which make it a key lineage to include in comparative work.

Many model and non-model plants have recently established CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing systems. Developing CRISPR in Ceratopteris is promising because C. richardii (and the Hnn strain) is diploid with a short life cycle and homozygotes can be easily created in one generation of gametophytic selfing (Shan et al., 2020). One potential avenue of study with CRISPR could be the apogamy pathway in C. richardii (Bui et al., 2017), investigating the connection between apogamy and spore number in C. richardii. This species produces 16 spores per sporangium, a number often indicative of apogamy in ferns (Grusz, 2016); C. richardii reproduces sexually but apogamy can be easily induced. If a CRISPR system could be established in Ceratopteris, one might be able to extend such technology to other members of the Pteridaceae known for apogamy (Grusz et al., 2021; Grusz, 2016; Grusz et al., 2009), or for application in other non-model ferns.

## The environmental influence on development

Ceratopteris richardii is a well-known model system for studying sex determination (Banks, 1997) and the alternation of generations in homosporous plants (Eberle et al., 1995). However, there are some steps in its life cycle that are poorly understood. Almost nothing is known about how Ceratopteris gametophytes are established in the wild. It is unknown if Ceratopteris spores must germinate on soil, or if they can germinate and establish gametophytes in standing or slow-moving water.

Recently the effect of soil bacteria on sex determination in C. richardii was investigated for the first time (Ganger et al., 2019). In the presence of a soil bacterium, there were more hermaphroditic (compared to antheridiate) gametophytes as well as increased growth (Ganger et al., 2019). Ceratopteris uses an antheridiogen pheromone system to control sex determination (Scott and Hickok, 1987; Banks, 1997), and soil bacteria may be influencing sex determination in a similar way. Additional experiments would benefit our understanding of how natural conditions might affect gametophyte establishment and sex determination in Ceratopteris, outside of the known role of antheridiogens. The establishment of new plants is particularly important as climate change is a threat to the current habitat of Ceratopteris, both as sea levels rise and rainfall becomes less predictable.

In addition to the establishment of new plants, climate change may influence the morphology, ecology, and physiology of Ceratopteris. There is dramatic variation in frond morphology within Japanese C. thalictroides based on the growing season length (Masuyama, 1992); such intraspecies variety has not been systematically characterized in any other species in the genus. This is important to understand because leaves have been used by some authors as the primary method of identification in Ceratopteris (Benedict, 1909; Lloyd, 1974), despite this being one of the most variable traits. Understanding the model species C. richardii and its relatives in the wild is important for conservation efforts, as well as to understand what natural variation exists in these species that may be informative to future work.

## Systematics and hybridization

Hybridization among Ceratopteris species is well-documented (Hickok and Klekowski, 1974; Nakazato et al., 2007; Hickok, 1977; Hickok, 1973), and these hybrid taxa as well as progenitor species can be morphologically cryptic (Adjie et al., 2007). Lloyd predicted the presence of multiple cryptic lineages in C. thalictroides, but detecting these taxa was not possible at the time without genetic analysis (Lloyd, 1974).

During the 1990s and early 2000 s, Masuyama and colleagues examined cryptic variation within C. thalictroides from Asia and Oceania. They used a combination of work on allozymes and cross-breeding experiments (Masuyama et al., 2002), chromosome counts (Masuyama and Watano, 2005), morphology of wild and cultivated plants (Masuyama and Adjie, 2008; Masuyama, 1992), along with plastid and nuclear markers (Adjie et al., 2007) to describe three cryptic species (Masuyama and Watano, 2010). More recently, Zhang et al. described another cryptic species of C. thalictroides endemic to Hainan Province in China. This taxon, Ceratopteris shingii, has some unique characteristics in the genus: a creeping rhizome, terrestrial growth on volcanic rock, and is sister to all other species in the genus (Zhang et al., 2020). Its phylogenetic placement and unique characteristics could provide some new hypotheses for trait evolution and an updated perspective on the life history and ecology of the genus.

In addition to the diversity of Ceratopteris in Asia, the Americas may have novel cryptic species. Natural hybrids between C. thalictroides and C. pteridoides have been described in South America (Hickok and Klekowski, 1974), as well as synthesized hybrids between several New World species (Hickok, 1973; Hickok, 1978). Kinosian et al., found several hybrid individuals and potentially a cryptic species of C. thalictroides in the Americas (Kinosian et al., 2020a). Interestingly, the same study did not find distinct wild populations of C. richardii. Future work on systematics in the group should focus on detangling cryptic species and identifying the extant range and phylogenetic placement of C. richardii.

A robust evolutionary tree is particularly important for Ceratopteris following the publication of the C. richardii genome. The taxonomy of model organisms is not always fully understood until after they become model systems (e.g., Arabidopsis, Al-Shehbaz and O’Kane, 2002; Rattus norvegicus, Musser et al., 2005 and Caenorhabditis elegans, Denver et al., 2003; De Ley, 2006), and C. richardii is no exception.

Despite having unique characteristics like a distinct deltoid leaf shape and only 16 spores per sporangium (Lloyd, 1974), C. richardii is not often identified correctly. For example, specimens identified as C. richardii from Central and South America, as well as western Africa, are each more genomically similar to other species than they are to one another (Kinosian et al., 2020b). This could be due to misidentification of collections, a poor understanding of its native range, or the extinction of C. richardii in the wild. This last possible explanation is troubling because, as we discuss above, it is important to have wild populations to best understand the potential of model organisms. Revisiting the localities of known C. richardii collections (detailed in Lloyd, 1974) should be a goal for future fieldwork. New wild collections will help elucidate the outstanding questions about the taxonomy and natural history of C. richardii, but may also provide novel populations or strains to include in lab studies.

## Plant genome structure and evolution

On average, heterosporous plants have fewer chromosomes and smaller genomes than homosporous plants. Ceratopteris richardii is the first homosporous fern with the genomic resources to address why these differences between hetero- and homosporous genomes exist. Nakazato et al. generated a genetic linkage map for C. richardii which showed that it is likely not repeated rounds of polyploidization that leads to larger genomes in ferns, but rather small-scale gene duplications (Nakazato et al., 2006). More recently, Marchant et al. published the first draft genome assembly for C. richardii and found additional support for genetic diploidy and limited rounds of polyploidization (Marchant et al., 2019b). These data further support the theory that homosporous fern genomes are large not because of whole-genome duplication, but because they do not have the same mechanisms for genome downsizing as heterosporous plants (Clark et al., 2016; Szövényi et al., 2021).

The draft genome of Ceratopteris richardii is an important stepping stone for studying land plant evolution (Marchant et al., 2019b); a more complete genome is on the way that will be a better resource for genomic work (Marchant et al., 2022). A high-quality genome for C. richardii will also aid in the development of targeted enrichment or whole-genome resequencing. This latter advancement in sequencing resources for ferns will help us understand reticulate evolution and polyploidy in ferns, as phylogenies can be estimated with hundreds of genes.

In addition to the Ceratopteris richardii genome, there are many other fern genomes that have been recently published or will be available soon. Several heterosporous fern and lycophyte genomes have been published in the last few years, including the heterosporous ferns Azolla filiculoides and Salvinia cucullata (Li et al., 2018), and the heterosporous lycophytes Selaginella moellendorffii (Banks et al., 2011), S. lepidophylla (VanBuren et al., 2018), and Isoëtes taiwanensis (Wickell et al., 2021). In the near future, several additional homosporous fern genomes will be available, including Adiantum capillus-veneris (Polypodiales), Alsophila spinulosa (Cyatheales), Dipteris conjugata (Gleichinales), Ptisana robusta (Marattiales), Huperzia asiatica and Diphasiastrum complanata (Lycopodiales; Drs. F.-W. Li and M. Barker, personal communication). As more homosporous fern genomes become available, the preliminary work with the C. richardii genome will be tested in a more rigorous phylogenetic context, hopefully leading to a clearer picture of land plant genome evolution.

## Conclusion

Although Ceratopteris richardii has been used as a model for decades, fundamental aspects of its natural history are still unknown. A few examples include basic taxonomy, origins of spore number, salt tolerance, origins of polyploids, phenotypic plasticity, and intraspecies morphological variation (see Box 2). Many of these topics are ripe for undergraduate or graduate student projects and could be integrated into existing research programs to answer fundamental aspects of fern biology.

Additionally, C. richardii is a useful tool for teaching students at all grade levels about plant biology (https://www.c-fern.org/). As detailed by Marchant, the C-fern can be incorporated into curriculum topics ranging from basic plant biology to evolution and development to bioinformatics. In the lab, field, or classroom, the recently published C. richardii genome provides a new window into the study of this fern (Marchant et al., 2019b). As more fern genomic resources become available, having Ceratopteris as a well-established model system will only become more important to test novel hypotheses about land plant evolution.

The article should be useful for those interested in learning more about ecological and genetic diversity in the genus, which could be leveraged in understanding genotype – phenotype relationships in this species.

results.result: The taxonomic history and current classification of Ceratopteris is described, including its original description by Linnaeus (1764), renaming by Brongniart (1821), variable species counts (1-12), and current placement within Pteridaceae, one of the largest fern families.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by appropriate citations to primary taxonomic literature (Linnaeus 1764, Brongniart 1821, Lloyd 1974, PPG 2016) and reference to Figure 1 showing phylogenetic placement. These represent standard historical taxonomic facts that are appropriately documented.

results.result: Ceratopteris comprises approximately ten species distributed throughout tropical regions, growing in seasonally inundated areas. C. richardii specifically originates in the Caribbean and Western Africa and grows rooted or floating in shallow, primarily freshwater habitats.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C34-C37 are supported by multiple citations (Masuyama and Watano 2010, Zhang et al. 2020, Yu et al. 2021, Lloyd 1974, Warne and Hickok 1987) and visual evidence from Figures 2 and 3 showing distribution maps and habitat photos. The geographic and ecological descriptions are consistent with cited literature.

results.result: Classification of Ceratopteris species has been challenging due to inconsistent morphologies, requiring molecular methods to reconstruct phylogeny. Cryptic and hybrid species appear common in the genus.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 are supported by appropriate citations to molecular phylogenetic studies (Adjie et al. 2007, Kinosian et al. 2020a, 2020b). The need for molecular methods to resolve morphologically cryptic diversity is a well-established principle in plant systematics and is appropriately applied here.

results.result: C. richardii was developed as a fern model system in the 1960s-70s due to ease of laboratory cultivation and short life cycle. The Hnn strain (C-fern) from Cuba became widely used, and additional strains of C. richardii, C. thalictroides, and C. pteridoides have since been developed.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C15 are well-supported by extensive citations to historical literature from the 1960s-70s (Pal and Pal 1962, 1963; Klekowski 1970; Stein 1971; Hickok 1973, 1977; Hickok and Klekowski 1973, 1974; Lloyd and Warne 1978) and more recent strain development work (Nakazato et al. 2006, Muthukumar et al. 2013). This represents well-documented historical development of the model system.

results.result: Ceratopteris has become an important model for studying sex determination, apogamy, genome structure, hybridization, reproductive barriers, developmental biology, and transgenic studies in ferns over recent decades.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C22 are supported by multiple citations to relevant research areas (Eberle et al. 1995, Ganger et al. 2019, Atallah et al. 2018, Banks 1997, Bui et al. 2017, Cordle et al. 2010, Nakazato et al. 2006, 2007, Baniaga and Barker 2019, Hickok and Klekowski 1974, Adjie et al. 2007, Hou and Hill 2002, Conway and Di Stilio 2020, Sun and Li 2020, Aragón-Raygoza et al. 2020, Plackett et al. 2018, Bui et al. 2015, Cannon et al. 2018). The breadth of research applications is well-documented.

results.result: C. richardii is one of few spore-bearing model systems and the only vascular, spore-bearing, homosporous model species, making it a critical evolutionary lineage for comparative studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by citations to other spore-bearing models (Physcomitrella: Cove 2005, Rensing et al. 2008; Selaginella: Banks et al. 2011) and established knowledge about plant phylogeny. The unique phylogenetic position of C. richardii as the only homosporous vascular model is accurately stated and appropriately contextualized.

results.result: Ceratopteris has a large genome (~11 GB) and high base chromosome number (n=39), which has partly delayed development of genetic resources compared to other plant model systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 provide specific genomic data (11 GB genome, n=39 chromosomes) and infer a causal relationship between genome complexity and resource development. While the data are stated as facts, the causal inference (C28) is reasonable but not directly tested. The genome size and chromosome number are consistent with cited literature.

results.result: The first draft genome sequence for C. richardii was published by Marchant (2019), representing the first genome for a homosporous fern. C. richardii was chosen because it has a relatively small genome for a homosporous fern.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 are supported by citations to Marchant 2019a, Marchant et al. 2019b, and Sessa et al. 2014. The historical significance as the first homosporous fern genome and the rationale for species selection are appropriately documented.

results.result: A homosporous plant genome provides opportunities for comparative studies of alternation of generations, sex determination, and reproductive modes. A reference genome benefits development of new molecular markers for targeted or whole-genome sequencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 represent reasonable speculation (C32) and established knowledge (C33) about the utility of reference genomes. While C32 is speculative about future research opportunities, it is based on sound biological reasoning. C33 reflects standard applications of reference genomes in genomics research.

results.result: Acrostichum (sister genus to Ceratopteris) tolerates high salt levels in tidal habitats. Natural salt tolerance in Ceratopteris is not fully understood, but salt-tolerant mutants are easily generated in the lab.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by appropriate citations (Zhang et al. 2013, Medina et al. 1990, Chasan 1992, Warne et al. 1995). The acknowledgment of incomplete knowledge about natural salt tolerance (C39) is appropriate, while the ease of generating lab mutants (C40) is documented.

results.result: Ceratopteris inhabits ephemeral water sources. C. richardii has a short life cycle of approximately 120 days, much shorter than the annual or multi-year life cycles typical of most ferns.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are supported by citation to Stein 1971 for the specific 120-day life cycle and established knowledge about typical fern life cycles. The comparative statement (C43) is reasonable given general knowledge of fern biology.

results.result: The fern life cycle exhibits alternation of generations between diploid sporophyte and haploid gametophyte, with both generations completely independent at certain stages. This differs from bryophytes (sporophyte dependent on gametophyte) and seed plants (gametophyte dependent on sporophyte), providing unique opportunities to study each generation separately.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 represent established knowledge about plant life cycles and are accurately stated. The comparative framework correctly distinguishes ferns from bryophytes and seed plants. The inference about research opportunities (C48) is reasonable given the biological facts presented.

results.result: Ceratopteris exhibits multiple reproductive modes including sporophytic outcrossing, gametophytic outcrossing, and gametophytic selfing. Evidence exists for both within-species outcrossing and among-species hybridization.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 describe reproductive modes based on established knowledge (C49-C51) and cite evidence for outcrossing and hybridization (C52-C53: Nakazato et al. 2007, Adjie et al. 2007, Kinosian et al. 2020a, Hickok and Klekowski 1974). The reproductive biology is accurately described and appropriately documented.

results.result: Fern outcrossing and gametophytic sex expression are controlled by antheridiogens, gibberellin-related pheromones released by archegoniate gametophytes to promote antheridiate development. This system confers outcrossing benefits similar to heterospory.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 represent established knowledge about fern reproductive biology (C54-C56) and cite support for the functional significance (C57: Bateman and DiMichele 1994, Hornych et al. 2021). The mechanism and evolutionary interpretation are appropriately documented.

results.result: Solitary Ceratopteris gametophytes can become bisexual and self-fertilize, theoretically allowing single-spore colonization. Apomixis can be induced in C. richardii in the lab. This life cycle variation makes Ceratopteris powerful for studying fern reproduction and provides an evolutionary reference for seed plant reproduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are supported by appropriate citations (Schedlbauer and Klekowski 1972, Cordle et al. 2007). The inference about single-spore colonization (C59) follows logically from bisexual gametophytes. The broader significance for comparative studies (C61-C62) represents reasonable inference from the documented reproductive flexibility.

results.result: Ceratopteris was developed as a model organism because it is easy to grow in lab settings, has a rapid life cycle, and is tractable for genetic transformations. However, model organisms chosen for convenience can be poor representative taxa.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 are supported by citations (Eberle et al. 1995, Hickok et al. 1995, Alfred and Baldwin 2015). The practical advantages for model system development are documented, and the cautionary note about representativeness (C66) is appropriately cited and provides important context.

results.result: Ceratopteris has unusual traits among ferns: it is semi-aquatic (rare among ~12,000 fern species), has an unusually short life cycle, and produces 32 or 16 spores per sporangium (versus typical 64). This reduced spore number often indicates apogamy, but no natural apogamous taxa are described in Ceratopteris. These characteristics make it a good model but not necessarily representative of all ferns.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C74 are supported by appropriate citations (PPG 2016, Stein 1971, Lloyd 1974, Grusz 2016). The comparative data on spore numbers are specific and documented. The paradox of reduced spore number without apogamy (C72-C73) is accurately noted. The conclusion about limited representativeness (C74) is a reasonable inference from the unusual characteristics described.

results.result: A reference ontogenetic framework for the Hnn strain detailing gametophyte and sporophyte development was recently published (Conway and Di Stilio 2020). Combined with transformation techniques, transcriptome, and genome resources, this provides necessary tools for comparative work.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by appropriate citations (Conway and Di Stilio 2020, Geng et al. 2021, Atallah et al. 2018, Marchant et al. 2022, 2019b). The integration of developmental framework with genomic resources represents an important advance for the model system.

results.result: Stable transgenic lines have been established in both gametophyte and sporophyte generations of the Hnn strain using three methods: tungsten microparticle bombardment of sporophytic tissue, Agrobacterium infection of haploid gametophyte tissue, and Agrobacterium infection of haploid spores.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by appropriate citations documenting the three transformation methods (Plackett et al. 2014, 2015a; Bui et al. 2015; Muthukumar et al. 2013). The availability of multiple transformation approaches in both generations is well-documented.

results.result: Gametophyte transformation provides unique perspectives on haploid gene function not easily studied in seed plants. Transformed gametophytes can self-fertilize to produce stable homozygous sporophytes, enabling comparative studies across land plants in both generations.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 represent reasonable inferences from established knowledge about fern biology and genetics. The unique advantages of working with independent haploid gametophytes are accurately described, and the ability to generate homozygotes through selfing is based on sound genetic principles.

results.result: Plackett et al. (2018) investigated LEAFY (LFY) transcription factor function in C. richardii using transgenic gametophytes and sporophytes. LFY is important for moss embryo cell division and angiosperm floral meristem development, but with no functional overlap between lineages. The study reported for the first time that LFY is required for C. richardii gametophyte development, suggesting this function was ancestral but lost in seed plants where gametophytes are reduced.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C92 are supported by appropriate citations (Plackett et al. 2018, Tanahashi et al. 2005, Carpenter and Coen 1990). The novel finding about LFY function in fern gametophytes (C90) is clearly attributed. The evolutionary inference (C91-C92) is reasonable given the phylogenetic position of ferns and the data presented, though it remains a hypothesis requiring further testing across lineages.

results.result: Apogamy can be induced in C. richardii, but the genetic mechanism was unknown until recently. Bui et al. (2017) identified a C. richardii ortholog of the flowering plant BABY-BOOM gene AINTEGUMENTA (CrANT) and created transgenic gametophytes with over- and knockdown-expression. This was the first such study in a non-seed plant and provides evidence for conserved apomixis gene function across land plants.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C100 are supported by appropriate citations (Cordle et al. 2007, Boutilier et al. 2002, Soriano et al. 2013, Bui et al. 2017). The identification of CrANT and experimental manipulation are clearly documented. The significance as the first non-seed plant study (C99) and evidence for conservation (C100) are appropriately stated, though the degree of functional conservation would benefit from additional comparative data.

results.result: Work on gene families in bryophytes, Selaginella, and seed plants does not always show functional overlap. Including Ceratopteris may provide functional or developmental links. Ferns are an independent lineage with unique characteristics that have continued evolving, but share characteristics with both bryophytes (spores, independent gametophytes) and seed plants (vasculature, independent sporophytes), making them key for comparative work.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C107 are based on established knowledge (C101-C102, C105-C106) and reasonable speculation (C103). The citations (Plackett et al. 2015b, McDaniel 2021) support the view of ferns as an independent lineage. The inference about Ceratopteris as a key comparative lineage (C107) is reasonable given its phylogenetic position and shared characteristics, though the actual utility depends on specific gene families studied.

results.result: Many plants have established CRISPR/Cas9 systems. Developing CRISPR in Ceratopteris is promising because C. richardii is diploid with a short life cycle and homozygotes can be easily created in one generation. C. richardii produces 16 spores per sporangium (often indicative of apogamy) but reproduces sexually, though apogamy can be easily induced.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C112 are based on established knowledge about CRISPR technology (C108) and cite support for the advantages in Ceratopteris (C109-C110: Shan et al. 2020). The spore number data (C111) and reproductive mode (C112) are consistent with earlier claims and established knowledge. The potential for CRISPR development is reasonable speculation based on documented biological characteristics.

results.result: Almost nothing is known about wild gametophyte establishment in Ceratopteris, including germination requirements. Ganger et al. (2019) first investigated soil bacteria effects on C. richardii sex determination, finding more hermaphroditic gametophytes and increased growth in bacterial presence. Soil bacteria may influence sex determination similarly to the known antheridiogen pheromone system.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 appropriately acknowledge knowledge gaps. Claims C115-C117 are supported by citation to Ganger et al. 2019 with specific experimental results. The known antheridiogen system (C118) is documented (Scott and Hickok 1987, Banks 1997). The speculation about bacterial mechanism (C119) is reasonable but requires further experimental validation.

results.result: Climate change threatens Ceratopteris habitat through sea level rise and unpredictable rainfall, and may influence morphology, ecology, and physiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 represent reasonable inferences based on established knowledge about climate change impacts on tropical wetland habitats. While speculative about specific effects on Ceratopteris, the general threats from sea level rise and altered precipitation patterns to ephemeral wetland species are well-established in climate science.

results.result: Japanese C. thalictroides shows dramatic frond morphology variation based on growing season length, but such intraspecies variation has not been systematically characterized in other Ceratopteris species. Leaves have been used for identification despite being highly variable.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C125 are supported by citation to Masuyama 1992 for the documented variation in Japanese C. thalictroides. The acknowledgment of gaps in knowledge for other species (C123) is appropriate. The problematic use of variable leaf morphology for identification (C124-C125) is documented (Benedict 1909, Lloyd 1974) and represents a valid taxonomic concern.

results.result: Hybridization among Ceratopteris species is well-documented, and hybrid and progenitor species can be morphologically cryptic. Lloyd (1974) predicted cryptic lineages in C. thalictroides but lacked genetic tools. Masuyama and colleagues used allozymes, cross-breeding, chromosome counts, morphology, and molecular markers to describe three cryptic species.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C132 are supported by extensive citations documenting hybridization (Hickok and Klekowski 1974, Nakazato et al. 2007, Hickok 1977, 1973), cryptic species (Adjie et al. 2007), Lloyd's predictions (Lloyd 1974), and Masuyama's comprehensive work (Masuyama et al. 2002, Masuyama and Watano 2005, 2010, Masuyama and Adjie 2008, Masuyama 1992, Adjie et al. 2007). The multi-method approach to species delimitation is well-documented.

results.result: Zhang et al. described another cryptic species, Ceratopteris shingii, endemic to Hainan Province, China. This species has unique characteristics: creeping rhizome, terrestrial growth on volcanic rock, and is sister to all other species in the genus.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C136 are supported by citation to Zhang et al. 2020. The unique morphological and ecological characteristics and phylogenetic position are clearly documented. The sister relationship to all other species has important implications for understanding trait evolution in the genus.

results.result: Natural hybrids between C. thalictroides and C. pteridoides occur in South America, and synthesized hybrids between New World species have been created. Kinosian et al. (2020a) found hybrid individuals and potentially a cryptic C. thalictroides species in the Americas, but did not find distinct wild C. richardii populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C140 are supported by appropriate citations (Hickok and Klekowski 1974, Hickok 1973, 1978, Kinosian et al. 2020a). The failure to find distinct wild C. richardii populations (C140) is significant given its status as the model species and warrants the follow-up discussion about taxonomy and conservation.

results.result: Model organism taxonomy is not always fully understood when they become models. Despite unique characteristics, C. richardii is often misidentified. Specimens identified as C. richardii from different regions are more genomically similar to other species than to each other, possibly due to misidentification, poor understanding of native range, or wild extinction.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C144 are supported by citations to examples from other model organisms (Al-Shehbaz and O'Kane 2002, Musser et al. 2005, Denver et al. 2003, De Ley 2006) and genomic data for C. richardii (Kinosian et al. 2020b, Lloyd 1974). The genomic dissimilarity finding (C143) is significant and well-documented. The possible explanations (C144) are reasonable hypotheses that require further investigation, with the extinction possibility being particularly concerning.

results.result: Heterosporous plants average fewer chromosomes and smaller genomes than homosporous plants. C. richardii is the first homosporous fern with genomic resources to address these differences. Genetic linkage mapping and draft genome assembly support that large fern genomes result from small-scale duplications and lack of downsizing mechanisms rather than whole-genome duplication.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149 are based on established knowledge (C145) and supported by citations to genetic mapping (Nakazato et al. 2006) and genome assembly work (Marchant et al. 2019b, Clark et al. 2016, Szövényi et al. 2021). The evidence converges on a mechanism of genome size evolution distinct from polyploidization, though additional homosporous fern genomes will be needed to test generality.

results.result: The draft C. richardii genome is an important stepping stone for studying land plant evolution. A more complete genome is forthcoming that will better support genomic work and aid development of targeted enrichment or whole-genome resequencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C152 are supported by citations (Marchant et al. 2019b, 2022). The significance of the draft genome (C150) is appropriately stated. The forthcoming improved genome (C151) is documented. The speculation about future applications (C152) is reasonable based on standard uses of high-quality reference genomes.

results.result: Several heterosporous fern and lycophyte genomes have been published recently, and several additional homosporous fern genomes will be available soon, enabling more rigorous phylogenetic testing of genome evolution hypotheses.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C154 are supported by citations to published genomes (Li et al. 2018, Banks et al. 2011, VanBuren et al. 2018, Wickell et al. 2021) and personal communication about forthcoming genomes. The expanding genomic resources will enable more robust comparative analyses, though the specific species and timelines for C154 depend on ongoing projects.

results.result: Despite decades of use as a model, fundamental aspects of C. richardii natural history remain unknown. C. richardii is useful for teaching plant biology at all levels, from basic biology to bioinformatics. As more fern genomic resources become available, Ceratopteris as an established model will become increasingly important for testing hypotheses about land plant evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C158 appropriately acknowledge knowledge gaps (C155), document educational applications (C156-C157), and speculate reasonably about future importance (C158). The educational utility is supported by reference to c-fern.org. The speculation about increasing importance is reasonable given the expanding comparative genomic context.

results.result: Figure 1 shows three extant independent evolutions of heterospory in ferns and lycophytes. The Ceratopteridoid clade within Pteridaceae includes Acrostichum and Ceratopteris. C. froesii is absent from the phylogeny due to lack of genetic sequence data.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C161 describe Figure 1 content and are supported by the figure and citation (Bateman and DiMichele 1994 for heterospory evolution). The phylogenetic relationships shown are consistent with current understanding. The absence of C. froesii due to lack of sequence data is explicitly noted.
